toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

toolsAdded.name: fd
toolsAdded.description: Find files and directories by name with fd. Respects .gitignore by default. Results are limited to 1000 entries unless a higher limit is given; output is limited to 2000 lines or 50KB, and complete truncated output is saved to a temporary file.

pattern.description: Regex matched against file names (or a glob when glob is true). Omit to list everything under path.

path.description: Directory to search. Defaults to the current working directory.

type.description: Only return entries of this type: file, directory, or symlink.

extension.description: Only return files with this extension, e.g. 'ts' or 'md'.

glob.description: Treat pattern as a glob (e.g. '*.test.ts') instead of a regex.

hidden.description: Include hidden files and directories. Defaults to false.

limit.description: Maximum number of results (1-10000). Defaults to 1000.

toolsAdded.name: rg
toolsAdded.description: Search file contents with ripgrep. Uses smart-case matching, respects .gitignore by default, and returns at most 100 matches per file unless a different limit is given. Output is limited to 2000 lines or 50KB; complete truncated output is saved to a temporary file.

pattern.description: Regex to search for (literal text when fixed_strings is true).

path.description: File or directory to search. Defaults to the current working directory.

glob.description: Only search files matching this glob, e.g. '*.ts' or 'src/**'.

file_type.description: Only search files of this ripgrep type, e.g. 'ts', 'js', 'py', 'rust'.

case_sensitive.description: true forces case-sensitive matching, false forces case-insensitive. Defaults to smart-case.

fixed_strings.description: Treat pattern as a literal string instead of a regex.

hidden.description: Search hidden files and directories. Defaults to false.

context.description: Lines of context to show around each match (0-20).

limit.description: Maximum matches per file (1-1000). Defaults to 100.

toolsAdded.name: read_full
toolsAdded.description: Read a text file's entire contents in a single call, with NO truncation. Use this when you need to perform semantic analysis over a complete artefact and any sampling, chunking, or programmatic slicing would compromise the synthesis. The file is sent to your context window as one continuous string. Hard cap: 10 MB. For files over the cap, the tool returns a refusal message and you must fall back to the built-in `read` tool with explicit offset iteration. For ordinary code or config reading, prefer the built-in `read` tool — `read_full` is for the specific case where partial reads would defeat the task.

toolsAdded.name: web_search
toolsAdded.description: Search the web using OpenAI, Brave, Parallel, Tavily, Exa, Perplexity, or Gemini. Returns an AI-synthesized answer with source citations. OpenAI web_search uses a Codex subscription or OpenAI API key. For comprehensive research, prefer queries (plural) with 2-4 varied angles over a single query — each query gets its own synthesized answer, so varying phrasing and scope gives much broader coverage. When includeContent is true, full page content is fetched in the background. Searches auto-open the interactive browser curator and stream results live; set workflow to "none" to skip curation or "auto-summary" for a model-generated summary without the browser curator. Provider auto-selects: OpenAI when suitable and available, then Exa, Brave, Parallel, Tavily, Perplexity, Gemini API, then Gemini Web.

query.description: Single search query. For research tasks, prefer 'queries' with multiple varied angles instead.

queries.description: Multiple queries searched in sequence, each returning its own synthesized answer. Prefer this for research — vary phrasing, scope, and angle across 2-4 queries to maximize coverage. Good: ['React vs Vue performance benchmarks 2026', 'React vs Vue developer experience comparison', 'React ecosystem size vs Vue ecosystem']. Bad: ['React vs Vue', 'React vs Vue comparison', 'React vs Vue review'] (too similar, redundant results).

domainFilter.description: Limit to domains (prefix with - to exclude)

workflow.description: Search workflow mode: none = no curator, summary-review = open curator with auto summary draft (default), auto-summary = generate summary without opening curator

toolsAdded.name: fetch_content
toolsAdded.description: Fetch URL(s) and extract readable content as markdown. Supports YouTube video transcripts (with thumbnail), GitHub repository contents, and local video files (with frame thumbnail). Video frames can be extracted via timestamp/range or sampled across the entire video with frames alone. Falls back to Gemini for pages that block bots or fail Readability extraction. For YouTube and video files: ALWAYS pass the user's specific question via the prompt parameter — this directs the AI to focus on that aspect of the video, producing much better results than a generic extraction. Content is always stored and can be retrieved with get_search_content.

forceClone.description: Force cloning large GitHub repositories that exceed the size threshold

prompt.description: Question or instruction for video analysis (YouTube and video files). Pass the user's specific question here — e.g. 'describe the book shown at the advice for beginners section'. Without this, a generic transcript extraction is used which may miss what the user is asking about.

timestamp.description: Extract video frame(s) at a timestamp or time range. Single: '1:23:45', '23:45', or '85' (seconds). Range: '23:41-25:00' extracts evenly-spaced frames across that span (default 6). Use frames with ranges to control density; single+frames uses a fixed 5s interval. YouTube requires yt-dlp + ffmpeg; local videos require ffmpeg. Use a range when you know the approximate area but not the exact moment — you'll get a contact sheet to visually identify the right frame.

frames.description: Number of frames to extract. Use with timestamp range for custom density, with single timestamp to get N frames at 5s intervals, or alone to sample across the entire video. Requires yt-dlp + ffmpeg for YouTube, ffmpeg for local video.

model.description: Override the Gemini model for video/YouTube analysis (e.g. 'gemini-2.5-flash', 'gemini-3-flash-preview'). Defaults to config or gemini-3-flash-preview.

toolsAdded.name: get_search_content
toolsAdded.description: Retrieve full content from a previous web_search or fetch_content call.

responseId.description: The responseId from web_search or fetch_content

queryIndex.description: Get content for query at index

urlIndex.description: Get content for URL at index

toolsAdded.name: session_search
toolsAdded.description: Semantic search over past pi sessions. Returns summaries of the most relevant sessions for a natural language query. Use to find previous work, decisions, debugging sessions, or code changes.

project.description: Filter by project name or path substring (matches projectSlug or cwd, same semantics as session_list)

toolsAdded.name: session_list
toolsAdded.description: List past pi sessions with optional filters by project, date range, or archive status. Returns session metadata and summaries.

project.description: Filter by project name or path substring

after.description: Only sessions after this date (ISO format, e.g. 2026-03-01)

before.description: Only sessions before this date (ISO format)

toolsAdded.name: session_read
toolsAdded.description: Read the full conversation from a past pi session. Provide the session file path or session ID. Supports pagination for large sessions.

session.description: Session file path (from session_search/session_list results) or session UUID

offset.description: Start from this entry index (for pagination, default 0)

include_tools.description: Include tool results in output (default false, verbose)

toolsAdded.name: knowledge_search
toolsAdded.description: Semantic search over local knowledge files. Returns the most relevant file excerpts for a natural language query. Use for finding past notes, investigations, decisions, documentation, and context. Prefer this over grep when you need conceptual or fuzzy matching rather than exact text.

toolsAdded.name: kb_read
toolsAdded.description: Read a note from the knowledge base by name, relative path, or [[wikilink]]. Resolves fuzzy references without needing an absolute path — use this when you know the note's title/filename but not its full path on disk.

name.description: Note reference: filename, basename, relative path, or [[wikilink]]. Examples: 'evergreen/hybrid-search', 'Hybrid search.md', '[[Hybrid search]]', '[[evergreen/hybrid-search|alias]]'.

max_bytes.description: Truncate output to at most this many bytes (default 65536).

toolsAdded.name: memory_search
toolsAdded.description: Search persistent memory for facts, preferences, and project patterns the user has established across sessions.

toolsAdded.name: memory_remember
toolsAdded.description: Store a fact, preference, or lesson in persistent memory. Use dotted keys like pref.editor, project.rosie.lang, tool.sed.usage. For corrections, use type='lesson'.

negative.description: True if this is something to AVOID

toolsAdded.name: sign_document
toolsAdded.description: Prepend or merge an authorship manifest into a planning, intent, or architecture document. Markdown (.md) uses YAML frontmatter; HTML (.html/.htm) uses a `<!--pi-manifest ... -->` comment that browsers ignore. Records the current session id and name as a manager that future implementation agents can consult via consult_manager.

path.description: Path to the document to sign (relative to cwd or absolute).

role.description: What kind of authorship this is. Common values: intent, architecture, plan, manager.

name.description: Override for the human-readable session name. Defaults to the current session name.

toolsAdded.name: consult_manager
toolsAdded.description: Consult a read-only frozen manager snapshot for guidance on a meaningful decision the implementation plan does not resolve. Resolves the manager from `author` (explicit), `author_doc` (read manager_sessions from the doc's manifest — markdown frontmatter or HTML `<!--pi-manifest-->` comment), or the fallback binding, in that order. Returns a structured oracle answer with a confidence level. The oracle may say the snapshot does not resolve the question — that is a valid answer.

observation.description: The surprising fact in code or plan that triggered this consult. Be concrete.

decision.description: The specific decision being considered, in one sentence, phrased as a question with options.

options.description: At least two plausible options. Always include 'Escalate to the user' as one option. A single-option list is a sign you are rubber-stamping.

recommendation.description: Your current best option and a one-sentence reason.

blast_radius.description: What is annoying or expensive to reverse if your recommendation turns out to be wrong.

evidence.description: Optional file/line references, prior decisions, or test names that ground the observation.

author.description: Explicit session id or path to consult. Overrides author_doc and the fallback binding.

author_doc.description: Path to a planning/intent/architecture document (markdown or HTML). Its `manager_sessions:` manifest names the author to consult.

author_role.description: When author_doc has multiple manager_sessions, pick the one whose role matches (e.g. 'architecture', 'intent', 'plan').

toolsAdded.name: workstream_submit
toolsAdded.description: THE single terminal call for a T3 Code Workstream sub-thread: submit your markdown report plus a structured outcome, and the control plane derives what happens next — you never set your own lane at completion. Omit outcome (or pass 'done') for plain completion: the report is recorded and your plan advances to done in one step, releasing dependents — refused while you hold an attention flag you raised this turn, because completing would clear it (pass an outcome token instead and you yield with the flag standing). Pass outcome 'needs_human' to record the report and raise the needs_guidance flag instead (a human is pulled in; your lane is unchanged). Any other outcome token (e.g. 'rework_approach', or review verdicts like 'needs_rework'/'clean'/'fixed_inline' when you are in a review gate) is routed by the control plane; during an active rework round it routes back to the reviewer for re-verification, otherwise an outcome with no matching route YIELDS you to your live parent orchestrator with your report — escalation is the safe default, and you are NOT done in that case. The tool result echoes the routing decision: read it — 'yielded' or a rework route means you are NOT done.

markdown.description: The markdown report to hand back, stored on disk and shown to whoever receives your work next (your parent orchestrator, or the gate counterpart in a review loop). Make it a deliberate handoff: what you did, the key results and decisions, and anything the parent must act on, not a transcript dump.

outcome.description: Structured outcome token. Omitted ⇒ 'done' (plain completion). Reserved: 'done', 'needs_human'. Review-gate verdicts (reviewers): 'clean', 'fixed_inline', 'needs_rework'. During an active rework round, any non-'needs_human' token routes back to the reviewer; otherwise any unmatched token yields you to the orchestrator — use a short snake_case token like 'rework_approach'.

contested.description: Optional: findings you reject, verbatim-quotable — preserved on the audit trail (opaque to routing).

counts.description: Optional reviewer finding counts for the verdict chip (opaque to routing).

toolsAdded.name: workstream_request_attention
toolsAdded.description: Raise an attention flag on a T3 Code Workstream thread you own (this thread or one you directly spawned) — the single surface that pulls in a human. A raise HOLDS the work for that human; it is your turn's last act, not a label you attach to a report. The flag clears the moment the thread resumes or reaches done/cancelled, so completing yourself in the same turn erases the hold and releases your dependents — the submit path refuses a plain completion while your raise stands, and a raise on an already-finished thread is refused too. To hand a report back with the hold intact, pass a short non-'done' outcome to workstream_submit: the report is recorded and you yield to your parent, flag standing. Two reasons: 'awaiting_acceptance' means a human (or the parent acting for the human) must accept this thread's output before its plan may reach 'done' and its dependents release — it is NOT 'some reviewer thread should look at this' (a thread whose output flows to a separate reviewer thread just goes 'done', which releases that reviewer). 'needs_guidance' means you cannot proceed without a human — including when what you want is answers to your questions, which is guidance, not acceptance. Write the accompanying report for a human who has read none of this thread: explain the blocker without relying on internal labels or unseen reports.

threadId.description: Id of the thread to flag; defaults to the calling thread when omitted.

reason.description: Why a human is needed: 'awaiting_acceptance' (output needs human sign-off before done) or 'needs_guidance' (cannot proceed without a human).

toolsAdded.name: workstream_list
toolsAdded.description: List your workstream: the whole graph of threads in your orchestration tree (every node's id, role, title, plan lane, attention flags, spawn generation, parent, last-activity, and report/session file paths) plus lineage and waits-on edges. This is how you discover the ids of sibling/other threads you were not handed directly, so you can then consult them or read their report/session files.

toolsAdded.name: consult_thread
toolsAdded.description: GLOBAL read-only consult of another thread, answered from a frozen fork of that thread's session. It reaches ANY thread the server knows (across worktrees and projects), not just your workstream tree. Use it when the user points you at another thread — by name ("ask the liveness-detection thread …") or via an @-mention. Identify the target by exactly one of: threadId (preferred; an @-mentioned thread arrives in the message as [Title](thread://<id>) — pass that <id>), or name (a fuzzy sidebar-title match). If a name matches several threads it returns ranked candidates instead of guessing; surface them and confirm with the user, then call again with the chosen threadId. It never resumes or mutates the target; to push a message the target acts on, use notify_thread.

threadId.description: Exact id of the target thread. Preferred when known (e.g. from an @-mention [Title](thread://<id>)). Provide threadId OR name, not both.

name.description: Fuzzy sidebar title/name of the target thread. Used when you don't have an exact id; an ambiguous name returns ranked candidates to confirm with the user.

question.description: The question to answer from the target thread's frozen session context. That fork shares none of your context, so make the question self-contained: name what you are asking about rather than referring to your own thread's state.

toolsAdded.name: set_thread_title
toolsAdded.description: Rename THIS thread's own sidebar title in T3 Code. You pass only a title; the thread is always resolved from the session, so you can only ever rename yourself — never another thread or a child. Use it to keep the sidebar legible: e.g. when a root's auto-from-first-message title is unhelpful, or when a child's scope has sharpened into something more specific than its spawn title. This does not touch the goal (use goal_update for that).

title.description: The new sidebar title for this thread (non-empty).

toolsAdded.name: goal_task_list
toolsAdded.description: Read the task tree of THIS thread's active goal (the shared tree, resolved from the session — you never pass a goalId). Use it for orientation and reconciliation: the tree injected into your prompt is a snapshot from your spawn and is never refreshed, so a child may have marked its task done or added discovered work your snapshot does not reflect. If you are anchored to a branch, this returns THAT branch in full — its checklist block is the exact text a branch rewrite takes — preceded by the read-only spine showing where it hangs; pass scope "tree" for the complete goal, which is what an unanchored thread always gets and the only complete source for a whole-tree rewrite. This is a read — it mutates nothing. Errors cleanly if this thread has no active goal.

scope.description: "branch" (default when you are anchored): your anchor's subtree in full, preceded by the read-only spine showing where it sits. "tree": the complete goal task tree.

toolsAdded.name: goal_task_add
toolsAdded.description: Append ONE task to the task tree of THIS thread's active goal — a targeted, concurrency-safe write that touches only the task it creates, so it is safe to fire mid-flight while others hold the tree. The goal is resolved from the session — you never pass a goalId, and you can only ever mutate your own thread's goal. Use it to record a single discovered actionable item (e.g. 'evaluate whether to fix pre-existing bug X') as a short imperative work item, nested under the task or theme it belongs to. It lands in your own branch by default when you are anchored; any task of the goal is a legal explicit parent, so work you discover elsewhere enters the shared tree the moment you find it — the echo shows where it landed, with its ancestors. To add several items at once, or to reshape your branch, use goal_tasks_rewrite instead. Errors cleanly if this thread has no active goal.

text.description: A short plain-language work item naming the outcome (at most 300 characters) — never a finding, verdict, or status note; details go in reports or memos.

parentTaskId.description: Id of an existing task in this goal to nest the new task under. Omit to add under your own anchor (or, unanchored, as a new top-level phase/theme).

toolsAdded.name: goal_task_update
toolsAdded.description: Update ONE existing task in THIS thread's active goal: rename it (text) or mark it done / reopen it (done) — a targeted, concurrency-safe write that touches only that task, so it is safe to fire mid-flight while others hold the tree. The goal is resolved from the session; the taskId must belong to it, and when you are anchored it must be in your own branch — a task outside it is refused. This is how a thread marks its OWN task done the moment it finishes the work. Re-nesting, reordering and removing a task are not here: they are edits via goal_tasks_rewrite.

taskId.description: Id of the task to update; must belong to this thread's goal.

text.description: New task text: a short plain-language work item naming the outcome (at most 300 characters) — never a finding, verdict, or status note; details go in reports or memos.

done.description: Mark the task done (true) or reopen it (false).

toolsAdded.name: goal_tasks_rewrite
toolsAdded.description: Replace what you own in THIS thread's goal task tree with the markdown you submit — the primary structural mutation. Restructure, re-nest, reorder, merge, rename, mark done, and prune in ONE call: submit the revised tree in the same `- [x] text (id)` checklist form goal_task_list returns. Lines keeping an existing task's `(id)` ARE that task (its text, done-state, parent, and order become what you submitted; its creation time is preserved); lines without an id are new tasks; tasks you omit are deleted. Indentation (two spaces per level) is the nesting, so a cycle is unrepresentable. Scope follows ownership: the thread that owns the goal submits the WHOLE tree; an anchored thread submits exactly its BRANCH — one top-level line carrying its anchor's id plus everything beneath it, leaving the rest of the goal untouched. Rewrite from a fresh goal_task_list read at that scope, since anything added since your last read and left out is lost. Rejected for a child with no anchor: the tree's owner does the restructuring.

markdown.description: The complete revised tree at your scope (the whole goal, or your own branch rooted at your anchor) as an indented markdown checklist, one task per line: `- [ ] Open task`, `- [x] Finished task (task-id)`. Two spaces of indent per level of nesting; keep the trailing `(id)` on every retained task; omit it for new tasks. New or changed text must be a short plain-language work item naming the outcome (at most 300 characters), never a finding, verdict, or status note; details go in reports or memos.

toolsAdded.name: enable_toolset
toolsAdded.description: Activate a dormant tool family in THIS session. Your role runs with a deliberately lean default tool surface; the full catalogue stays registered but inactive until enabled. Families: 'delegation' — the workstream graph-authoring and child-management tools (spawn, scaffold, brief, gates, release, stop, prompt, lanes, dependencies, plus notify_thread, thread_fork and the goal handoff/continue/update tools) for handing work to a child — independent pieces your work splits into, or a bounded, context-heavy sub-phase of your own brief; 'human-input' — ask_user_question, for a fork that is genuinely irreversible, destructive, or purely the user's preference, where a structured question beats a needs_guidance attention flag; 'browser' — all browser_* tools, for live web/UI driving and verification; 'studio' — the studio_* REPL and export tools; 'all' — every registered tool (escape hatch). Activation applies from your next step and adds the enabled tools' own usage guidelines to your system prompt, so enable first, then act. Enable a family only when the task in front of you actually needs it — the lean default is deliberate. Enablement lasts until the session restarts; simply re-enable if the tools go dormant.

content.text:
You are a planner sub-thread spawned by a parent orchestrator in T3 Code.

Your brief:
# Write the Phase 1 merge runbook: `docs/upstream-sync/29-cadence-pull-9-phase1.md`

## Situation

Loom (this repo, `QuinRiva/loom`) is a Pi-first fork of `pingdotgg/t3code`. Upstream's Orchestration V2 (`de34391427` + follow-ups to `upstream/main`, now `1a3f7ad508`) deleted `apps/server/src/orchestration/` — the V1 engine Loom's workstream/goal layer is welded to — and replaced it with `orchestration-v2/` plus a native Pi adapter. Carl has decided, in a signed strategy document, to **re-platform**: take `upstream/main` as the base and re-express Loom's orchestration layer on V2 in later phases. **Phase 1 is the mechanical merge, upstream winning on structure.** You write the runbook coders will execute for it. A reviewer gates your runbook against the strategy before any coder starts.

## Read first, in this order

1. `plans/upstream-pull9-strategy/plan.mdx` — the signed authority (revision 3). Read it in full; the sections that bind Phase 1 hardest are "Where the Loom layer lives after pull 9" (the FileTree), the verdict table, the hunk inventory, "The genuine collisions", "Phase 1 — mechanical merge, upstream wins on structure" and its gate, the "Silent failures" callout, and "Decisions recorded". When a Phase 1 decision is not settled by it, use `consult_manager` with `author_doc` pointing at this file before guessing, and record the answer (with its confidence) in the runbook.
2. `docs/upstream-sync/28-pull9-v2-alignment/04-trial-merge-surface.md` — the real trial merge of `upstream/main@a1d9d72aef` onto the pull-8 branch: every conflicted path classified (155 textual, 95 modify/delete, 86 directory-rename relocations, 2 add/add), ~125 dangling-import files, 92 removed contract names used by 241 files, the 117 silently auto-merged files of which 8 lost an exported name, `config.ts` auto-merging to `statev2.sqlite`. `docs/upstream-sync/28-pull9-v2-alignment/02-loom-inventory.md` is the Loom-side inventory (what each Loom module is and what it depends on) — use it to classify Loom-only files.
3. `docs/upstream-sync/27-cadence-pull-v0.0.45-pre-orchestration-v2.md` — the pull-8 runbook; your document follows its structure. Read §1–§2 (topology, invariants, departures), §5 (per-zone doctrine, protected list), §6 (pre-ruling format), §8–§9 (sequencing, gate checklist), §10 (decision-log `DL-n` format; it reached DL-79 — continue the numbering from DL-80 so ids stay unique across docs), §11 (recorded failure modes), §13 (tooling), and the Session 1–3 write-ups to see what a session hand-off looks like. `docs/upstream-sync/25-cadence-pull-v0.0.43-nightly-20260920.md` is pull 7's equivalent. `recaps/pull8-decisions/recap.mdx` holds Carl's pull-8 rulings (DL-72–79) that carry forward.
4. `docs/upstream-sync/05-strategy.md` §4.3 — the doctrine that governs every hunk decision: *Carl decides functionality; where upstream now expresses the same functionality, upstream's mechanism is the baseline and Loom's variant is deleted.*
5. `docs/upstream-sync/pull7-tools/` — the tooling (`hunks.sh`, `sideresolve.py`, `union.py`, `parsesweep.mjs`, `lostdecls.py`, `aliascheck.py`, `unmarkedsweep.sh`, `whatismissing.sh`, …). Read each script's header so the runbook tells coders exactly which to run when.

## Re-measure before you partition

The trial merge was against `a1d9d72aef`; `upstream/main` is now `1a3f7ad508`, ten commits later (including `06e627448b` MCP targets, `37de6cbde6` keyed lock, `7812230572` subagent PR links, `1beb0355d0` queued notifications), and this branch carries revision-3 docs the trial never saw. Re-run the trial merge in **your** worktree and abort it:

```
git fetch upstream main
git -c rerere.enabled=false -c merge.renameLimit=30000 merge --no-commit --no-ff upstream/main
# capture: git status --porcelain=v2, git ls-files -u, git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U, marker counts, then
git merge --abort
```

`rerere.enabled=false` matters: the shared `rr-cache` already holds unresolved preimages from the trial, and recording more is noise. Never `git stash` in this repo (shared `.git`). The runbook's zone partition is built from **your** re-measurement, with the delta from doc 04 stated. The trial's classification scripts may still be in `/tmp/pull9-trial/` (`classify.py`, `dangling.py`) — reuse if present; otherwise write the equivalent into `docs/upstream-sync/pull9-tools/` (new, committed, tiny).

## What the runbook must contain

Follow doc 27's shape. Specifically:

**Topology and invariants.** ours = this branch's tip, theirs = `1a3f7ad508`, merge-base `024d49520e`. Invariants coders must hold: every commit during the merge uses `--no-verify` (the pre-commit hook deletes `MERGE_HEAD`); `git rev-parse <merge>^2` must equal the upstream tip; never `git stash`; do not trust any `rerere` auto-resolution you did not make (check `git rerere status` / diff after merge); `pnpm-lock.yaml` is taken from upstream and regenerated by install, never hand-merged; `Migrations.ts` ends byte-identical to upstream's; every retained Loom hunk in an upstream-shared file carries a `// loom:` marker (`unmarkedsweep.sh` enforces). Check `cat "$(git rev-parse --git-dir)/t3code-setup-state.json"` before any install/typecheck.

**Zone partition — every conflicted path and every dangling-import file in exactly one zone**, in an appendix like doc 27's Appendix B. The structural zones the strategy dictates:

- *Quarantine.* The relocated Loom V1-engine files (86 in the trial) are moved **out** of `orchestration-v2/` into a tsconfig-excluded quarantine directory — "undone, not owned" — diffable during the port, deleted in Phase 4, **never compiled, never linted, never tested**. You choose the location and prove the exclusion mechanics: `apps/server/tsconfig.json` includes `src`, so a directory under `src/` needs an explicit `exclude`; check vitest's include globs, the lint config (`vp check` runs biome/oxlint/eslint — find out which and how to exclude), `unmarkedsweep.sh` and `lostdecls.py`. Loom's `apps/server/src/provider/Drivers/PiDriver.ts` (add/add, 2,959 lines) and the Pi support files under `provider/Drivers/Pi/` that only it uses go to quarantine; upstream's 195-line `PiDriver.ts` wins. `decider.loom.ts`, `projector.loom.ts`, `commandInvariants.loom.ts`, `goalTaskAnchor.loom.ts` go with the engine. `packages/contracts/src/orchestration.loom.ts` (1,795 lines, imports the deleted `orchestration.ts`) is removed from the build the same way (quarantine, or excluded — say which and why; it is a separate package with its own tsconfig).
- *Upstream's deletion wins.* The 95 modify/delete files (V1 engine, V1 provider adapters incl. `ProviderService`, V1 projection repositories, V1 contracts, `threadReducer`, queued-message web files, V1 tests). Loom's hunks in them are listed with the functionality each carried and the phase that re-expresses it, so nothing is lost silently — that list is part of the detach ledger.
- *Detach.* Loom-only files outside the engine that import a removed V1 module or contract name (the trial found ~25: `apps/server/src/loom/serverLayers.ts`, `loom/startup.ts`, `mcp/WorkstreamSpawnHttp.ts`, `mcp/GoalTaskHttp.ts`, `GoalHandoffHttp.ts`, `ThreadForkHttp.ts`, `UserInputHttp.ts`, `cli/goal.ts`, `provider/Drivers/Pi/askUserBroker.ts`, `persistence/Layers/SqliteLanes.ts`, …) and the Loom web/mobile/client-runtime modules that read `LoomThreadShellFields` or other removed contract names. **Phase 1 ports nothing.** Per the strategy, the REST `/provider-tools` routes are retired and web modules that read Loom shell fields are *excluded from the build, not stubbed*. Where a consumer cannot be excluded because an upstream-shared file imports it (e.g. `ChatView.tsx` rendering a Loom panel), the detachment is the smallest honest one: drop the import and the render site behind a `// loom:` marker, or leave a component that renders nothing — never one that lies about state. Each detachment is a **ledger row**: path, what it rendered or served, the V1 names it depended on, how it was detached (excluded / import dropped / renders nothing / quarantined), and the phase that re-hangs it (3a tools, 3b control plane, 3c driver, 3d web). Define the ledger's format and location (a section of doc 29, or a sibling file it names).
- *Non-orchestration Loom surfaces that survive* — the pull-8 rulings and the strategy's verdicts: migrations lane split (`LoomMigrations.ts` 1001+, `Migrations.ts` byte-identical), `Sqlite.ts` with `runAllMigrations` beside `initializeV2Database` (hunk inventory, Area K), thread search/embeddings and usage views **to the extent they do not depend on the V1 engine** — `ThreadEmbedder.loom.ts`, `ThreadSearch.loom.ts`, `Layers/embedding/*.loom.ts` are among the relocated files, so you must read their imports and rule: move to a Loom directory and keep compiling if they depend only on sqlite/messages/settings, else quarantine with a ledger row naming the phase that re-seams them. Also: ship script, dev-runner, setup-script runner on upstream's mechanism with Loom's breadcrumb hunks (DL-73), session reaper per DL-74 (V1 reaper is deleted upstream — rule on what survives), workstream web surfaces on upstream theme tokens (DL-79), sidebar v2, MDX plan/recap renderer (46 files, untouched), composer context/inline tokens, keybindings, settings hunks (`PiSettings.enabled` true, bundled pi, pi-only driver registry in `builtInDrivers.ts` — the strategy keeps these as Loom hunks; note upstream's PiDriver registers `PiAdapterV2`), `config.ts` → accept `statev2.sqlite` (Phase 1's gate requires it). Flag explicitly, in a short list the reviewer and I can scan, **every non-orchestration surface Phase 1 has to detach because it is welded to V1** — that list is what I escalate if it is surprising.
- *Textual zones* for the ~155 UU/AA files, pull-7 style, with per-zone doctrine and pre-rulings for the hard files: `ws.ts` (24 markers; V2 world wins, Loom's workstream WS methods go — `loom/wsMethods.ts` is a detach row), `serverRuntimeStartup.ts` (upstream's V2 recovery wins; Loom's 28 hunks are Phase 2/3b policy — ledger), `server.ts`, `client-runtime/src/state/*` (V2 shapes win), `ChatView.tsx`, `DiffPanel.tsx`, `composerDraftStore.ts`, `Sidebar*.tsx`, `ChatComposer.tsx`, `MessagesTimeline*`, `RightPanelTabs.tsx`, `settings.ts`, `rpc.ts`, `OrchestrationEventStore.ts`, `ProjectSetupScriptRunner.ts`, `AgentAwarenessRelay.ts`, `GitVcsDriverCore.ts`, `VcsStatusBroadcaster.ts`, `textGeneration/*` (incl. the `PiTextGeneration.ts` add/add), mobile. Pre-rule in doc 27 §6's format wherever the strategy's verdict table, hunk inventory or pull-8 rulings already decide the hunk; leave genuinely open hunks as explicit coder decisions with the doctrine question to ask.
- *Silently auto-merged files.* The 8 that lost an exported name (`McpSessionRegistry.ts`, `modelSelection.ts`, `mobile queries.ts`, `providerIconUtils.ts`, …) — re-measure with `lostdecls.py` against your trial and pre-rule each. `ChatMarkdown.tsx` (33 `loom:` lines, auto-merged) gets a review-by-eye instruction.

**Sequencing into coder sessions** (doc 27 §8 pattern), each handing off through the §10 decision log. Pull 8 ran: S1 merge resolved and committed; S2 typecheck from a fresh install; S3 gates/audits/smoke. Propose the split that fits a coder's context window — the structural zones (quarantine moves, modify/delete, detach ledger, dangling imports) are large but mechanical and may deserve their own session before or after the textual zones; say what state each session leaves (the merge **must** be committed with `MERGE_HEAD` intact at the end of the session that resolves the index — `git commit --no-verify`; later sessions commit fix-ups on top). Note for the boot-smoke session: it runs in its own T3 home (`--base-dir "$PWD/.t3"`), on a `VACUUM INTO` snapshot of `~/.t3/userdata/state.sqlite` (recipe in the repo `AGENTS.md` "Test data"; `secrets`/`settings.json` copied only as needed), lets V2 copy to `statev2.sqlite`, creates a project and a Pi thread, completes one turn with upstream's Pi adapter, restarts and confirms the thread resumes; never against `~/.t3/userdata`; kill only captured PIDs. Doc 27 Session 3 "Smoke evidence" shows how pull 8 drove its smoke — adapt it to V2 (what `pi` binary upstream's adapter resolves, `PiSettings.enabled`, how a thread is created and a turn sent without a browser if possible).

**Gate checklist** (doc 27 §9 shape): `vp run typecheck` and `vp check` green across every package with quarantine excluded; `vp test` for touched packages; `lostdecls.py`, `aliascheck.py`, `parsesweep.mjs` clean; `unmarkedsweep.sh` clean; `Migrations.ts` byte-identical to upstream; `git rev-parse HEAD^2` (of the merge commit) = `1a3f7ad508`; quarantine not reachable from any tsconfig/vitest/lint include; detach ledger complete (every dangling import resolved by a ledger row or a deletion); boot smoke as above.

**Failure modes** (doc 27 §11 shape), including the ones the strategy's "Silent failures" callout names that apply to Phase 1: the `config.ts` repoint (never boot against the live install), `rerere` preimages, the 117 auto-merged files, `lostdecls`, the pre-commit hook deleting `MERGE_HEAD`, pull-8's recorded mistakes.

## Out of scope — say so in the runbook

Phases 2–4: the sidecar contract, decider arm, toolkit, control plane, driver economics, web re-hang, data import, the deletions the plan schedules for Phase 4, cut-over, deploying. No PR. Phase 1 does not change behaviour of anything upstream shipped; it removes Loom's V1-welded surfaces from the build and records where they went.

## Done

`docs/upstream-sync/29-cadence-pull-9-phase1.md` (plus any `pull9-tools/` scripts) committed on your branch with `--no-verify` is fine for docs; sign it with `sign_document` (role `plan`). Work autonomously toward the outcome this brief is meant to deliver — stay anchored to the value it produces (the capability, fix, or decision), not just the mechanical steps. Keep the work focused and report progress clearly.
If you run a command you expect to take much longer than ~5 minutes (a full pipeline, a corpus classification, a long build or test suite), declare its expected duration so your parent is not spammed with slow-tool notices: prefix the bash command with an inline `# eta: <n>m` comment (e.g. `# eta: 25m — full corpus classification`, or `# eta: 1h`). The notices are then deferred until your estimate elapses; a declared `timeout` on the call is used as a fallback signal.
Finish with ONE call: `workstream_submit` — its description is the contract for outcomes and routing, and its result names where your report went. Write the report as a concise handoff for your parent orchestrator, not a transcript dump: lead with the value you delivered and what it enables or unblocks, then the key results/decisions and anything the parent must act on.
If a HUMAN is needed, raise it with `workstream_request_attention` — its description covers the two reasons and why a raise HOLDS your work rather than labelling your report. Do not sit silently halted: complete your work, or raise — never both in the same turn, because completing clears your own raise; your parent is woken automatically either way.

# Pull 9 strategy — adopt Orchestration V2, re-express Loom on top

Loom is a Pi-first fork of `pingdotgg/t3code` whose product is an orchestration layer: goals, a shared task tree, and a workstream graph of durable threads with roles, briefs, dependencies, review gates, attention flags, a plan position per thread (held or released, and whether the work is accepted as done — separate from whether it is running), liveness detection, isolated worktrees with fan-in, reports, and consult/notify. Upstream has now shipped **Orchestration V2** (commit `de34391427`, 1,914 files) with a native Pi adapter, and deleted the V1 engine Loom's layer is welded to. This document decides, area by area, whether upstream is heading where Loom is heading — and therefore whether Loom adopts upstream's mechanism and re-expresses its guarantees on it, or keeps its own — then rolls that up into one mechanism for pull 9.

**Done** means Carl has recorded a verdict on each of the twelve areas below and answered what remains open, so a follow-on planner can write the implementation plan for the chosen phases. This is revision 3: Carl has chosen the mechanism and settled every question the earlier revisions asked (recorded below); pull 8 has merged and deployed; the per-area verdicts have been re-checked against the pull-8 review reversals and the doctrine rule they produced; and Carl's parallel review of upstream's 41 orchestration tools against Loom's (`docs/upstream-sync/28-pull9-v2-alignment/05-upstream-toolkit-account.md`, `recaps/upstream-toolkit-vs-loom/recap.mdx`) is folded in — its explicit decisions as decisions, its 43 per-tool verdicts as defaults Carl accepted without working every card.

<Callout tone="decision">
**How to review this.** Each area ends in a `ReviewChoice`; Accept means the verdict and cost class stand, Reject means the follow-on plan must take a different path for that area (say which in the note), Discuss parks it. Silence accepts the recommendation. The decisions Carl has already recorded are listed under *Decisions recorded* and are not re-asked; the two confirmations still open (retiring the staging hold; how much of worktree isolation to carry) are in the form at the bottom. Card colour is triage only: **blue = adopt upstream**, **amber = hybrid**, **purple = retain Loom, re-expressed on V2**, **grey = retain Loom as-is because upstream has nothing there**.
</Callout>

## The recommendation in one paragraph

**Re-platform, staged.** Take `upstream/main` as the base including V2 and the Pi V2 adapter, and re-express Loom's layer as a V2 extension: Loom's thread fields, commands and events as a sidecar contract on V2's store; Loom's decider rules as a delegation arm (redesigned for V2's per-thread locking, not ported) plus a bounded, enumerated set of marked hunks in upstream's decider and dispatch core; Loom's control-plane workers (dispatcher, fan-in, liveness, exhaustion resume) re-seamed onto V2's event stream and shell snapshot; Loom's agent tools moved from bespoke REST routes onto upstream's MCP bridge as a Loom toolkit, with upstream's `delegate_task` family **withheld** from Loom threads so there is one delegation model in every prompt. The evidence says upstream is heading to the same destination as Loom on the *substrate* — durable children as real threads, event-sourced commands with receipts, a durable outbox, restart reconciliation, a shared tool bridge, a separate fork migration ledger — and to a genuinely different (or absent) destination on the *workflow*: no plan axis, no dependencies, no gates, no goals, no human holds, no liveness, no per-child worktree. Adopting the substrate and retaining the workflow is therefore the right split. "Retain" is not a cheap alternative: V2 rewired the web, mobile and client-runtime around V2 contracts and gates `/ws` on protocol version 2, so keeping V1 means freezing the whole client and the store mobile app, i.e. a hard fork. The staging is a feature freeze on Loom's orchestration layer, production staying on pre-pull-9 Loom, a long-lived integration branch, and a cut-over gated by a real Pi workstream smoke test. Pull 8 has landed and is in production, so the integration branch starts from it.

The rule that decides every area is the one pull 8's review wrote into `docs/upstream-sync/05-strategy.md` §4.3: *for each Loom hunk that differs from upstream's approach, ask who decided the difference. Carl decides functionality; an agent often chose the mechanism incidentally. Preserve the intent, not the incidental choice: where upstream now expresses the same functionality, upstream's mechanism is the baseline and Loom's variant is deleted, however much work it represented.* Every "retain Loom" verdict below names the functionality Carl decided and the guarantee upstream's nearest mechanism fails to meet; where it cannot, the Loom mechanism goes.

## What the evidence says, in five facts

The four research reports in `docs/upstream-sync/28-pull9-v2-alignment/` are facts-only; these are the five that carry the decision. Upstream code is cited at the reports' snapshot `a1d9d72aef` except where a fact comes from the toolkit account (report 05), which is pinned to `7812230572` — eight commits later, five touching `orchestration-v2/` or `mcp/`. One of those, `06e627448b` (#15219, "T3 MCP tools take explicit thread and project targets"), changes facts this document relies on: thread reads are environment-wide rather than project-scoped, cross-thread writes are gated by mid-turn and modes rather than project, `t3_thread_configure` targets any writable thread rather than only the caller, and `McpInvocationScope` gained a `requestNamespace` and a not-yet-issued client-caller kind. None of it changes a verdict — it widens what the withheld upstream tools could do, which is a reason for withholding, not against — but it is why the phase sketch re-merges upstream at every phase boundary rather than assuming a frozen target.

1. **V2 is an execution-fidelity model for one conversation, not a workflow engine.** Children share the parent's worktree; there are no dependencies, no staging, no cascade cancellation of app-owned children, no gates, no goals or tasks, no stall detection, no human holds; a role is a one-sentence prefix; the parent is woken with a generic "call `task_status`" pointer (`01-upstream-v2-inventory.md`, §A, §D, §E, §I and the closing *Design centre of gravity*).
2. **Loom is physically separated from V1 files but semantically welded to V1's vocabulary.** 24 commands, 25 events, a `goal` aggregate, about 35 projection columns, 45 migrations, about 20 snapshot-query methods, 8 in-place decider edits and 3 engine-invariant changes (`02-loom-inventory.md`, §0 "One structural fact"). The control-plane workers are portable modules on narrow seams.
3. **The Pi driver decision is downstream of the V2 decision.** Upstream's Pi adapter implements `ProviderAdapterV2`; Loom's implements the deleted V1 shape. If V2 lands, Loom's driver must be rewritten against V2 anyway, and upstream's adapter *is* that rewrite, fixture-tested on pi 1.0.0 (`03-pi-driver-comparison.md`, Headline 1).
4. **The merge is a merge plus a port, whatever the strategy.** 336 conflicted paths: 155 textual (pull-7 shaped, fits the pull-7 tooling) and 181 structural (95 modify/delete, 86 directory-rename relocations) with nothing on the other side to merge into; about 57,000 Loom lines sit on the deleted engine; 92 contract names used by 241 files vanish; about 125 files end up with dangling imports; `config.ts` silently auto-merges to `statev2.sqlite` (`04-trial-merge-surface.md`).
5. **Pull 8 removed only the pre-V2 drift** (348 to 336 conflicts in the dry runs), and the V2 surface is unchanged in size. Pull 8 has since merged (PR #323) and is in production; the merge-base with `upstream/main` is unchanged at `024d49520e`, so the trial-merge counts stand in shape, but they were measured against #323's tip, and `origin/main` has since gained #325 (99 files, the review reversals — notably the workstream web surfaces re-homed onto upstream's theme tokens, which touches the same files the web conflict count covers). Partly.** Upstream and Loom agree that a delegated child is a *real app thread* with a transcript a human can open and message (V2 `creationSource:"mcp"` children take messages; `02-loom-inventory.md` §A intent), that its parentage is recorded, and that launching into a prepared worktree is a server workflow with progress and retry (`ThreadLaunchService`, `01-upstream-v2-inventory.md` §A "Held / staged creation"). They disagree on everything above that: V2 has no dependency or ordering between children, no held lane, no cascade cancellation of app-owned children, no per-child worktree for delegated tasks, and merge-back is context not code.

**Verdict — hybrid.** Adopt V2's `AppThread` + `lineage` (`parentThreadId`, `relationshipToParent:"subagent"`, `rootThreadId`) as the parentage record, and V2's `message.dispatch` as the kickoff primitive. Retain Loom's graph semantics as an extension: `blockedBy`, the collapsed plan axis (`held`, `outcome`, `kickoffAt` — Area C), `spawnGeneration`, `graphKey`, `isolation`, `fanInState`, `routes`, `anchorTaskId`, `kickoffBriefPath`, `reportPath` in a Loom sidecar record keyed by thread id (not as fields on `AppThread`: V2 threads are full-row upserts and `makeSubagentChildThread` spreads the parent into children, so fields there would leak into upstream's child and fork paths — upstream itself had to stop children inheriting PR links in `7812230572`); `thread.spawn` / `thread.scaffold` / `thread.dependencies.set` / `thread.release` / `thread.outcome.set` / `thread.fanin.set` as Loom commands in the decider arm; the dispatcher's promotion rail and the fan-in reactor as Loom reactors on `streamDomainEvents`.

Two things follow that are easy to miss:

- **Loom children are not V2 "delegated tasks".** `delegated_task.request` requires a blocking parent run owned by the calling provider instance (`parent_not_active`), publishes — once — the child's most recently finished run at the moment the child first goes quiet, and never reopens (`SubagentProjection.ts:243–254`; report 05 §1.10 corrects the earlier "first run" paraphrase). Those invariants — the live-turn requirement, the absence of edges, the pointer result — contradict Loom's control-plane-created, dependency-gated, re-engageable children. (That a delegated child shares its parent's checkout is *not* a contradiction: Carl does not count per-child worktrees as a Loom requirement, below.) So Loom never uses `delegate_task` or `OrchestrationV2Subagent` rows for workstream children; the Loom `thread.spawn` arm nests upstream's `thread.create` with lineage set (the command has no lineage fields today, so the arm sets them the way `dispatchDelegatedTaskRequest` does) and emits Loom events in the same transaction. V2 already uses this nesting pattern internally (`Orchestrator.ts:9884` "nested: dispatchDelegatedTaskRequest already writes child events").
- **V2's `subagent` lineage carries upstream behaviour Loom must accept or hunk, item by item.** Sidebar filtering (`filterSidebarV2VisibleThreads`) matches Loom's "children are invisible in the sidebar" — accept. Thread notifications are suppressed for subagent threads (`ThreadNotificationCoordinator.tsx`) — accept; Loom surfaces children through the attention rollup. Subagent threads are dropped from navigation shells (`client-runtime/src/state/threadShell.ts`) — accept; Loom's thread tabs and board are the navigation. Titles are reformatted for subagents (`models.ts`) — hunk, Loom titles are manual. The awareness relay is silenced for them (`AgentAwarenessRelay.ts`) — accept. Separately, `streamStoredEventsFrom(afterSequence)` offers replay that V1's `streamDomainEvents` lacked; the dispatcher's full idempotent pass stays (it is the right design) but its catch-up machinery shrinks.
- **V2 locks per thread; V1 was one serial fibre.** Loom's arm today writes to many threads in one transaction because V1 processed every command on a single queue. V2 dispatches under `threadDispatch.withLock(threadId)`, reads one thread's projection, and upstream warns the keyed executor is neither reentrant nor deadlock-aware (`Orchestrator.ts:9878–9894`); upstream only ever nests into a thread it has *just created*. So the cancel cascade (writes to descendants), gate traversal (writes to the coder from the reviewer's submit) and gate resolution (both parties `done`) cannot be "one transaction" on V2. The mechanism this document commits to: **the arm writes only to the commanded thread** (and to threads it creates in the same command), recording the *decision* as a Loom event there (`route-taken`, `cascade-requested`); **the dispatcher turns the decision into one idempotent per-thread command per affected thread** under that thread's own lock, with deterministic ids and receipts, re-driven on every pass until the read model shows it applied. Because V2 receipts rejections and a repeated id is `PreviouslyRejected`, a re-drive command that is *not yet applicable* (the target is mid-steer, a merge-back transfer is pending, `/compact` is in flight) must not be rejected: it returns the same deferred error the `start_if_idle` hunk passes through without a receipt, so the next pass tries again. The zero-event hunk covers "already applied"; the deferral covers "not yet". Atomicity becomes eventual consistency with a window of one dispatcher pass; the rails already tolerate exactly that (they are idempotent passes over the full graph). An ordered multi-lock was rejected because upstream's executor gives no deadlock guarantee and Loom would be the only caller holding more than one key.

**What survives, and what does not simplify.** Survives: the dependency gate (every dependency's `outcome` is `done`), the brief gate (an unbriefed scaffold node does not start — this is the hold Loom actually relies on), and the kickoff, which stamps `kickoffAt` on the child's own thread; cancel cascade (the arm records the cascade on the cancelled thread; the dispatcher issues `run.interrupt` + `outcome: cancelled` per live descendant); subtree archive/delete cascade (hunks on V2's `thread.archive|unarchive|delete`, same pattern); honest per-turn diffs (start-of-turn baseline — attaches to V2's `checkpoint.captured` rather than the deleted `CheckpointReactor`; **more** important, not less, once children share a checkout, because sibling edits must fall outside this thread's turn diff). **Worktree isolation becomes an option, not a guarantee.** Carl's preference: a shared checkout is fine, and per-child isolation existed to keep the diff panel coherent. So the default for every role is the parent's checkout — upstream's model — and the guarantee this document previously listed ("dependents start from a tree containing merged output") holds trivially when there is nothing to merge. Everything that served isolation — `isolation` on the sidecar, `WorkstreamFanInReactor` (1,026 lines), the reaper (459), the provisioner's branch naming `ws/<parentBranch>/<role>-<id8>` and dirty-parent snapshot commit, `fanInState` as a dependency condition — is an **opt-in** (`isolation: "isolated"` at spawn) whose port is sized separately and is not on the pull-9 critical path (bottom form). **The staging hold is a retirement candidate.** `staged` / `workstream_release` (and with them the `held` bit of the collapsed axis) existed so a whole graph could be laid out and reviewed before any token was spent; that use is already served by scaffolding nodes without briefs — a node does not start until its brief is written, and the board shows it as not started — so the hold is a second mechanism for one effect. Pending Carl's confirmation (bottom form), `held`, `workstream_release` and the `staged` spawn parameter go, the collapsed plan axis is `outcome` + `kickoffAt`, and the import maps a V1 `planned` thread as not-started (it starts when its brief and dependencies allow, as any other). **`goal_handoff` is fixed, not re-expressed.** Today it creates a goal plus a root *held* for the human's first send and *without* a worktree; Carl rules both defects. Under V2 the new root is launched through upstream's `ThreadLaunchService.launch` with `workspaceStrategy: {type: "worktree", baseRef}` — the same substrate `t3_thread_launch` uses — so it starts immediately in its own worktree with the setup script run; `goal_continue` keeps sharing the caller's worktree, which is right. A phase-3 item. **Worktree provisioning for isolated children keeps Loom's call site** (when the option is used). V2's `defer_start` only parks a run in `preparing` and records the strategy (`Orchestrator.ts:5158–5171`); the worktree and setup work run in `ThreadLaunchService`'s private `schedulePreparation`, reachable only through `launch` (a new top-level thread) or `retryPreparation`. A promoted child dispatched with `defer_start` would wait in `preparing` forever. So `WorktreeProvisioner` provisions at promotion as today and writes `branch`/`worktreePath` via `thread.metadata.update` before the kickoff dispatch; exposing upstream's preparation for an existing thread is a possible later hunk, not part of pull 9. Pull 8's DL-73 already put the provisioner on upstream's setup-script runner (sentinel completion, idle-shell close) with Loom's breadcrumb and 30-minute breadcrumb timeout as marked hunks, and DL-54 made it honour `worktreeSubmodules`; both carry over unchanged — the functionality Carl decided there is "agents can poll a breadcrumb and a hung script does not hang them forever", which upstream's runner still does not provide. `forkFrom` (acknowledge-then-fork) is decided in Area L.

**Users gain** lineage in upstream's panel and mobile sheets and provider-neutral children (any V2 adapter). **Users lose** cross-thread atomicity: a cascade or gate resolution lands over one dispatcher pass rather than in one write, which is observable on the board for a moment and recoverable by construction.

**Cost class — redesign for the attachment, port for the workers; smaller than revision 2.** The shared libs (`workstreamDependencies.ts`, `workstreamGraph.ts`) move with logic intact; the fan-in reactor (1,026 lines), reaper (459), provisioner and `workstreamIsolation.ts` are off the critical path (an opt-in port only if Carl chooses it in the bottom form); `goal_handoff`'s root gains upstream's launch workflow instead of Loom's provisioner. The decider arm and the dispatcher's write path are a **redesign**: the arm loses its multi-thread writes and the dispatcher gains the per-thread re-drive for cascade, gate traversal and resolution.

## Area B — Agent tool surface and transport

**Same destination? Yes.** Both servers write a T3-owned pi extension at session open, pass it with `--extension`, and give it a per-session bearer from the same `McpSessionRegistry` credential; both forward `pi.registerTool` calls to the server over HTTP (`03-pi-driver-comparison.md` Headline 2, §2). Loom's `T3_WORKSTREAM_ENDPOINT` is literally upstream's MCP endpoint minus `/mcp`. The difference is contract: upstream is a real MCP client with dynamic `tools/list` discovery and `mcp__t3-code__*` names; Loom is a static list of 23 hand-authored tools POSTing to bespoke `/provider-tools/*` REST routes with server-rendered text.

**Verdict — adopt upstream's transport and its tool names, retain Loom's catalogue; withhold upstream's orchestration toolkit from Loom threads.** Loom's tool definitions (`providerToolDefs.ts`, 1,003 lines of description, snippet, guidelines, schema, `errorMode`) become a `WorkstreamToolkit` (and `GoalToolkit`) registered on `/mcp` beside upstream's ten toolkits, gated by the `workstream` capability Loom's driver already requests. The handlers (`WorkstreamSpawnHttp.ts` 4,061, `GoalTaskHttp.ts` 428, `GoalHandoffHttp.ts` 333, `ThreadForkHttp.ts`, `UserInputHttp.ts`) already talk to the engine only through `engine.dispatch` (14 sites) and five snapshot reads, so the port is at the edge: route → toolkit handler, `engine.dispatch` → `OrchestratorV2.dispatch`, `getShellSnapshot` → V2's `getShellSnapshot` joined with Loom's sidecar. Upstream's MCP tool `description` carries Loom's prose; the bridge's generic one-line guideline is replaced by the def's `promptSnippet` via a small hunk in `piT3McpExtensionSource.ts`. **Names follow upstream** (Carl's decision): agents call `mcp__t3-code__workstream_submit`, `mcp__t3-code__goal_task_add` and so on, exactly as upstream's bridge names every discovered tool. That is the doctrine applied to a mechanism an agent chose — the bare names were never a decision of Carl's — and it buys zero naming hunks in upstream's extension source at the price of a one-off text rewrite: every built-in role under `roles/`, project roles under `.t3code/roles/`, the pi-craft skills that name tools (`workstream-review-gate`, `ship`, `handoff`, the MDX skills' answer paths), the work-model addendum in the driver, `AGENTS.md`, the tool descriptions themselves where they cross-reference each other (`workstream_submit`'s text names `workstream_request_attention`; `enable_toolset`'s digest names the delegation family), and Carl's persistent memories that name a tool. The sweep spans three places, not one repository: this repository (roles, `.t3code/roles/`, this repository's `skills/` — `workstream-review-gate`, `ship`, the MDX skills — the work-model addendum, `AGENTS.md`, the tool descriptions), the pi-craft repository (`~/pi-craft/plugins/pi-craft/skills/`, where `handoff` and the authored-document skills live), and Carl's persistent memory store. Two tool descriptions also change meaning, not just name: `notify_thread`'s ("delivery never interrupts … a busy recipient has it queued", "must never … steer") is rewritten for steer-or-start, and `workstream_set_lane`'s becomes `workstream_set_outcome`. The gate: a search for the 24 bare names in each of the three places returns hits only in historical docs under `docs/upstream-sync/` and `plans/`, and a Pi smoke in which an agent reads its own tool list and calls `mcp__t3-code__workstream_submit` unprompted.

The genuine collision is **`delegate_task` / `t3_thread_*` beside `workstream_spawn` / `notify_thread`**: both surfaces land in one prompt unless one is filtered. Resolution has two halves, because upstream's `tools/list` is **not** filtered by capability: every toolkit is registered unconditionally (`McpHttpServer.ts:715–730`), the capability check happens only at call time (`OrchestratorMcpService.requireCapability`), and the pi bridge registers everything it lists. (1) For Loom-launched sessions the credential is issued with `workstream` and `pull-requests` (plus `preview` when browser tools are allowed) and **without `orchestration` or `worktree`** (one hunk in `McpSessionRegistry.issue`, which `06e627448b` has since reshaped), so `delegate_task` — which would create a child inside the parent's live turn only, with no gate, no edges and a pointer result — **fails if called** with `capability_denied`; so do `t3_thread_launch`, project CRUD, the environment and attachment tools, `t3_thread_update`, `t3_worktree_list` (which needs `orchestration` too) and, with `worktree` withheld, `t3_worktree_handoff` and `t3_worktree_status`. (2) Loom's own extension applies the role tool profile with `pi.setActiveTools` at `session_start`, and the profile omits upstream's orchestration and thread toolkits, so they are **not in the prompt** — this is what actually keeps them out, and it must run after the bridge's own `session_start` re-registration (an ordering to verify in phase 3a). The shared orchestration instructions that describe `delegate_task`, `create_threads`, `t3_thread_launch` and `schedule_task` — and tell pi to prefer native subagents — **cannot** be keyed on the capability from inside the extension: the extension holds only an endpoint and a bearer and cannot read the credential's capabilities, and the file is generated per instance, not per thread. ## Area C — Lifecycle and state model

**Same destination? Partly.** V2's `Run` / `RunAttempt` / `ExecutionNode` / `ProviderSession` states and the shell's `activityRunStatus` are a more honest **runtime axis** than Loom's derived `executing / starting / idle / none` projection over V1 session + latest turn, and V2's settle/snooze/wake model is the one Loom already adopted in the sidebar rehome. V2 has **no plan axis**, **no attention axis**, and **nothing** that detects a running turn making no progress (`01-upstream-v2-inventory.md` §C "Stuck runs, idle and stall detection").

**Verdict — adopt the runtime axis; collapse the plan lane to `held` + `outcome` and move `yielded` into attention (Carl's decision); retain attention, the dispatcher rails, liveness and Loom's restart-recovery rules as an extension; two hunks in V2's dispatch/receipt core are certain, not conditional.**

- **The plan axis, collapsed (Carl's decision).** Loom's six-value *plan lane* (`planned → ready → in_progress → yielded → done | cancelled`) is replaced by three facts that cannot desync. `held` (boolean): the staging hold — `true` means "in the plan, not released to run"; `workstream_release` clears it for a subtree. `outcome` (`done | cancelled | null`): whether the work is accepted-complete (`done` releases dependents and triggers fan-in), abandoned (`cancelled`, terminal, non-releasing), or neither; written by `workstream_submit`'s routing, by `workstream_set_outcome` (the renamed `set_lane`, for a parent or human forcing `done`/`cancelled` or reopening with `none`), and by the gate pass. `kickoffAt` (timestamp or null): when the control plane delivered the first turn — the only stored "has started" fact, so an imported thread or a human-started one reads correctly without consulting V2 runs. The board's columns are **derived**: *held* (`held`), *blocked* (not held, a dependency's `outcome` is not `done`), *ready* (not held, deps done, `kickoffAt` null), *in progress* (`kickoffAt` set, `outcome` null), *done*, *cancelled*. The former `yielded` lane — "parked for the orchestrator's decision" — was an attention flag whose audience is an agent, misfiled as a plan position; it becomes the attention reason **`awaiting_orchestrator`**.
- **Attention.** The stored set is `error | awaiting_acceptance | needs_guidance | awaiting_orchestrator`, plus the derived `awaiting_approval | awaiting_input | brief-needed`. Authority: `error` and `awaiting_orchestrator` are control-plane-only (the `server:` command-id guard works unchanged on V2 command ids); agents raise only `awaiting_acceptance` and `needs_guidance`; derived reasons are recomputed at the read boundary from V2's `pendingRuntimeRequest` and Loom's brief-needed predicate — nothing stored, nothing to erase.
- **What the collapse removes.** The kickoff no longer writes a lane in the same transaction as the first turn (`kickoffAt` is stamped by the dispatcher on its own thread before it dispatches); the "§7 unifying rule" shrinks from "every turn start clears all attention and reverts `ready`/`yielded` to `in_progress`" to "every turn start clears stored attention" (which already clears `awaiting_orchestrator`); the sticky-terminal rule is trivially true because a turn start never touches `outcome`; the gate's reopen is `outcome := null` on the coder (Area D); `workstream_set_lane`'s four-value enum becomes `workstream_set_outcome {done, cancelled, none}` beside the existing `workstream_release`; the historical `thread.status-set` remap is irrelevant because Loom data is not replayed under V2. Dependencies test `outcome == done` (and `fanInState: completed` for isolated dependencies) exactly as they tested the lane. The settlement blockers read `awaiting_orchestrator` where they read `yielded`. Agent-facing text still says "in progress", "ready" and "done" — those are the derived columns' names, and `workstream_list` renders them.
- **Turn-start rules** (clear stored attention on a human- or control-plane-originated turn start or steer; supersede an open question; started-dependents warning on reopen; **the first-turn dependency gate on every dispatch path** — a human message to a scaffolded child whose dependencies are not `done` must not start it, which today lives in a `thread.turn.start` hunk) become **one hunk cluster in V2's `message.dispatch` case** — the single place every run begins — replacing today's spread across `thread.turn.start`. Smaller than before the collapse: no lane revert, no sticky-terminal check.
- **Human stop raises `needs_guidance`, orchestrator stop does not** → hunk in `run.interrupt` keyed on the command-id prefix, as today.
- **Control-plane wakes: steer when steerable, with a tier split (Carl's decision) — and what the deferral hunk is still for.** Carl sees no reason to prefer Loom's `requireIdle` over upstream's rule (steer into a steerable turn, else queue, never interrupt) and wants a tier split: **FYI digests queued; yields, attention raises and gate verdicts steered.** The steered tier is upstream's `auto` as it stands. The queued tier is where the mechanism question lives, because V2's `queue_after_active` has two properties Loom's digests cannot accept: a queued run is frozen text, so three children finishing during one parent turn would queue three digests where Loom's rail would have delivered one recomputed digest; and V2 marks every queued run `queueHeld` on restart recovery and after a failed provider run (`ProviderRuntimeRecoveryService.ts:~281–290`), so a digest queued across a restart sits until a human issues `queue.resume`. The smaller correct answer for the queued tier is therefore still the deferral: a Loom `dispatchMode:{type:"start_if_idle"}` whose busy-parent outcome is a distinguished *deferred* error that `dispatchWithReceiptEffect` lets through **without writing any receipt** — V2 receipts every outcome, including rejections, and a repeated id is `PreviouslyRejected` (`:9710–9800`), so any receipt here would mean the parent is never woken (risk 7) — and the dispatcher recomputes the digest and retries on the next pass. On an idle parent the mode resolves to `queue_after_active`, which starts at once (nothing to queue behind, `shouldQueue` at `:4696`) and lets the message carry V2's `notification` (which upstream rejects on any other mode). This is one marked hunk at the dispatch/receipt boundary, and it is certain. The steered tier adds one requirement the earlier revisions did not have: the attention bookkeeping that rode the turn start (clear stored attention) must also run on `steer_active`, so a yield steered into a running orchestrator clears the child's `awaiting_orchestrator` the same way a fresh turn would — part of the same `message.dispatch` hunk cluster.
- **Automated wakes do not erase a hold.** A PR-watch wake (on from pull 9) and, if ever exposed, a schedule fire are `message.dispatch` turn starts carrying a `notification`. Loom's rule clears stored attention on turn start; applied to these it would erase a shipper's `awaiting_acceptance` on the first failing check, or a human's `needs_guidance` on an hourly schedule. Decision: the `message.dispatch` hunk clears agent-raised attention only for human- and control-plane-originated dispatches (`createdBy: user`, or Loom's `origin`), **not** for notification-source dispatches. A hold is a human-facing fact; a machine event should not remove it. This is also the reason bound schedules stay closed even with the rule in place: they would start turns the dispatcher never authorised.
- **Quiescence as completion (adopted upstream semantic).** Upstream treats a delegated child as complete the moment it first goes quiet. Loom children sometimes finish and forget `workstream_submit`; today the idle "forgot to finish" backstop waits out a grace window and raises `needs_guidance`, pulling a human in for a child that stopped one call short. The adopted shape: when the dispatcher's idle rail finds a child idle, with no stored attention, `outcome` null, no non-terminal children of its own and no open user-input request, past its grace window, it writes the child's last assistant message to the report file under a synthesised header, records `thread.work.submit` on the child's behalf with the reserved outcome **`quiescent`**, and `routeWorkSubmit` routes it as an unmatched outcome — **yield to the parent**, never `done` ("no outcome can ever silently become `done`" stands). A gate member that goes quiet yields too; its synthesised message is not a verdict. The grace window is keyed on **who started the child's last turn**, read from V2's message `createdBy` (and the shell's `latestUserAuthoredMessageAt`): a turn a human started gets a long window or none — Carl may be reading the answer — while a turn the kickoff, a `workstream_prompt` or a control notice started gets the short one. The timer is not new: it is the existing dispatcher pass (coalescing worker plus periodic tick) comparing activity freshness against the window, exactly as the idle backstop does today; this replaces that backstop's `needs_guidance` raise rather than adding a rail. No upstream hunk; one reserved token in `workstreamGraph.ts` and a rail change.
- **Zero-event success — the second certain hunk.** V2 rejects any command that produces no domain events (`"Command produced no domain events."`, `:9762`) and receipts the rejection. Loom's unchanged-value guards (a set-style command that changes nothing emits nothing but persists an *accepted* receipt — each redundant echo once cost a 1.5 s dispatcher pass, and one fan-in retry raised the same flag 13,420 times) would all become rejected tool calls. The hunk: for Loom command types, zero events is an accepted outcome with a receipt. Scoped to Loom's types so upstream's invariant is untouched for its own commands.
- **Settlement blockers** (`awaiting_orchestrator` attention, any descendant whose `outcome` is null; a root with a terminal `outcome` settles promptly; human send unsettles) → hunk in V2's `thread.auto-settle` case and `ThreadSettlementService`. Same shape as today.
- **Liveness sweep** (dead / waiting / stalled / spinning, 60 s cadence, one informed nudge then escalate) ports as-is; its heartbeat is written from the V2 adapter event stream (`provider-turn.updated`, `turn-item.updated`) into a Loom table instead of from V1 ingestion.

- **Restart recovery is Loom policy on V2's recovery service, and continuation must be switched on.** V2's `continueThreadsAfterServerUpdate` decodes to `false` by default and its continuation prompt is only "Continue where you left off." (`RestartContinuation.ts:22`). Loom's 28 marked hunks in `serverRuntimeStartup.ts` — a flagged, cancelled or approval-parked thread is not continued; a never-delivered kickoff is re-delivered verbatim rather than "continued"; stale-session reconciliation — become a Loom policy module on `ProviderRuntimeRecoveryService` / `RestartContinuation`, and the setting defaults to `true` for Loom (a settings hunk). Without this the no-silent-halt invariant does not survive a server restart.
- **The pending-steer stash stays.** V2 moved *queued* messages server-side, but a steer pi has already accepted lives in pi's process and dies with it; V2 does not track it. Loom's stash (`pendingSteering.ts`, 42 lines) rides the Loom continuation prompt as today, fed from the V2 adapter's steer path instead of V1 ingestion.

**What is verified before deletion.** Stuck-launch CAS repair (`stuckLaunchRecovery.ts`, 427 lines + decider case) and `thread.turn-start.fail` (40) addressed two V1 failures: a pi that hangs at spawn so the session sits in `starting` with no turn, and a `provider-turn.start` effect that fails before `turn.started` so the pending-turn row holds the idle gate forever. V2 has no watchdog for a run wedged in `starting` (nothing in `orchestration-v2/` detects it; upstream's `6108ef3d3d` fixes session-release record races and retries, not this), and under `start_if_idle` a wedged `starting` run counts as busy — which recreates the 16-hour gate stall the V1 code fixed. So the verification is concrete: kill pi at spawn and fail the start effect on a copied database under V2, and keep both modules unless the effect outbox's attempt retry provably recovers each case. Loom's exhaustion resume stays regardless (V2's `limitRecovery` covers provider usage limits, not Loom's per-account failover targets), re-anchored on V2's run error.

**Users gain** V2's run/attempt detail in the timeline and the settle/wake polish. **Users lose** nothing, provided the two dispatch-core hunks and the recovery policy land; without them the no-silent-halt invariant is not preserved.

**Cost class — redesign** for the collapsed plan axis and the axes' hooks (new attachment points, fewer rules), port for the rails and sweep. The collapse touches the dispatcher's predicates, the arm, the board's column derivation, two tool definitions and the role/skill text — all of which the prefixed-name sweep (Area B) is rewriting anyway, which is why doing it now costs less than it would alone.
